title: Governor of Alaska

context.text: Open seat: Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) is term-limited. Alaska uses a nonpartisan top-four primary (August 18, 2026) and ranked-choice voting in the general election.

Primary results: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) 22.5%, Democrat Tom Begich 20.8%, Bernadette Wilson (R) 10.0%, Dave Bronson (R) 8.1%, Treg Taylor (R) 7.3%. Begich withdrew after the primary, so fifth-place finisher Taylor advanced to the fourth ballot spot.

The Alaska Public Offices Commission recommended against certifying Taylor over his financial disclosure and Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom declined to certify him on August 31, briefly elevating his running mate Candice English; on September 4 Dahlstrom reversed course and certified Taylor, citing a Department of Law review.
President Trump endorsed Bernadette Wilson at an October 13 Wasilla rally and said the other Republicans should have dropped out; Bronson said he will remain in the race.

candidates.name: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins
candidates.ballotNote: Running with Zac Johnson, an Anchorage Assembly member listed on the ballot as nonpartisan. Finished first in the top-four primary.

summary.text: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is a Democrat from Sitka who served ten years in the Alaska House of Representatives and was a member of a bipartisan House coalition. His campaign focuses on school funding, fisheries and rebuilding the state ferry system, and he has said he would fill his cabinet one-third each with Democrats, independents and Republicans.

background.text: Born and raised in Sitka, Alaska; attended Yale University but dropped out to run for the Alaska House.
Served in the Alaska House of Representatives for District 35 (Southeast Alaska) from 2013 to 2023; chaired House State Affairs in the 30th Legislature.
Co-chaired a bipartisan working group on the state's fiscal crisis late in his legislative tenure.

priorities.text: Fix public schools: adequate state education funding and forward funding, so that school districts know their state funding by February or March.
priorities.quote: Number one, fix our schools. Public education is on the brink in Alaska, and in so many communities.

priorities.text: Rebuild the state ferry system with new vessels and independent, non-political management.
Seek a temporary moratorium on new data centers in Alaska until the Legislature passes a regulatory framework.

record.text: Prime sponsor of House Bill 216, which made 20 Alaska Native languages official state languages; it was signed into law (Chapter 116, SLA 14) on October 23, 2014.

candidates.name: Bernadette Wilson
candidates.ballotNote: Running with Mike Shower, former Alaska Senate minority leader. Top Republican vote-getter in the primary; endorsed by President Trump.
candidates.currentRole: Owner of Denali Disposal; conservative activist and former radio host

summary.text: Bernadette Wilson is an Anchorage business owner who has not held elected office. She owns the trash-collection company Denali Disposal, previously directed the Alaska chapter of Americans for Prosperity, and has worked on more than a dozen political campaigns. She advocates paying the Permanent Fund dividend under the statutory formula and has criticized relying on bipartisan legislative coalitions.

background.text: Born on the Kenai Peninsula and raised in Anchorage; great-niece of former Gov. Wally Hickel; owns Denali Disposal.
Hosted a talk-radio show until 2015; worked as Alaska director of Americans for Prosperity and for the Alaska Policy Forum.

Worked on more than a dozen campaigns, including Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson's and a 2010 ballot measure requiring parental notification of a minor's abortion; advised Rep. Nick Begich's 2024 campaign; campaigning for a ballot measure to repeal ranked-choice voting (as of May 2025).

priorities.text: Pay out full Permanent Fund dividends according to the statutory formula.
Says the state has not made progress on infrastructure and education under multiple administrations.
priorities.quote: We're at the bottom of education, the same place we were years ago.

priorities.text: Opposes large data centers in Alaska.
priorities.quote: I will never allow Alaska to be littered with hyperscale data centers that take our resources and spoil our lands.

candidates.name: Dave Bronson
candidates.ballotNote: Running with Josh Church, a financial professional. Finished fourth in the primary (8.1%).

summary.text: Dave Bronson is a Republican retired Air National Guard officer and commercial pilot who served as mayor of Anchorage from 2021 to 2024 and later managed Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport. He supports a constitutional amendment mandating Permanent Fund dividends by the pre-2017 formula and describes data centers as an economic opportunity.

background.text: Born in Superior, Wisconsin; B.S. in agricultural economics from the University of Wisconsin–Madison.
Served in the U.S. Air Force (1981–1990) and Alaska Air National Guard (1993–2005), retiring as a lieutenant colonel; works as a commercial pilot.
Elected Anchorage mayor in a May 2021 runoff, serving until 2024; later managed Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport and announced his resignation in August 2025.

priorities.text: Increase spending on infrastructure and the Permanent Fund dividend, including a constitutional amendment to mandate a dividend by the formula used from 1982 through 2016.
Encourages data centers, saying he sees economic opportunity in them.
priorities.quote: I'm a big believer in data centers.

candidates.name: Treg Taylor
candidates.ballotNote: Running with Candice (Candi) English, an oil and gas support business owner. Advanced to the fourth ballot spot after Tom Begich withdrew; certification was denied on August 31 and restored on September 4.

summary.text: Treg Taylor is a Republican lawyer who served as Alaska attorney general under Gov. Mike Dunleavy from 2021 until August 2025. The Department of Law participated in more than 80 legal challenges involving federal actions during his tenure, according to his campaign. His campaign emphasizes expanding resource development and working across party lines.

background.text: Attended the U.S. Air Force Academy; B.A. in political science (2001) and J.D. (2004) from Brigham Young University.

Worked in commercial litigation and as counsel for McKinley Capital Management and ASRC Energy Services; joined the Alaska Department of Law as deputy attorney general over the Civil Division in 2018.
Became Alaska Attorney General in 2021 (acting from January 30; confirmed May 11, 2021) and chaired the bipartisan Attorney General Alliance.

priorities.text: Expand resource development, including mining, timber and oil and gas drilling, to create economic opportunity.
Communicate more with the Legislature and the public and work across party lines.
Attract data centers that bring their own energy.

positions.summary: As attorney general, challenged federal restrictions on so-called ghost guns.

Ran television ads about transgender children in school sports in which he promised to “save girls’ sports”; the Dunleavy administration pushed for the ban on transgender girls on girls’ school teams during his tenure.

record.text: As attorney general, Taylor's tenure included court challenges to federal actions: he defended ConocoPhillips' Willow project on the North Slope, challenged federal ghost-gun restrictions and opposed COVID-19 vaccine mandates.

researchNotes: The Alaska Division of Elections certified candidate list (page updated September 25, 2026; loaded with TLS verification disabled because of a certificate error on the site) confirms exactly four tickets on the general-election ballot: Bronson/Church, Kreiss-Tomkins/Johnson, Taylor/English and Wilson/Shower. Treg Taylor is certified with running mate Candi English; the earlier English/Jodi Taylor ticket was superseded on September 4. Certified write-in candidates are not listed. Ballotpedia was unreachable (bot challenge). Bernadette Wilson's campaign site was a placeholder and she did not respond to interview requests, so her issue coverage is limited. Few documented stances map onto the fixed issue list, so positions are sparse by design. Officeholder records for Bronson and Taylor rely on news reports and Wikipedia rather than official pages. Running mates are listed in each candidate's ballot note, not as separate entries. The general election uses ranked-choice voting.
